criteria.criterion: A new file under docs/design/ cites throughput review 20261110-024838-mch9 and quotes the measured 2203.6 of 2252.0 median minutes per landed job from THROUGHPUT.md.
criteria.evidence: docs/design/direct-main-landing.md is new. Its 'Source' line and section 1 cite 20261110-024838-mch9 and quote '2203.6 of the 2252.0 median minutes per landed job'. These match evidence/records/throughput-reviews/2026-11/20261110-024838-mch9.json (window_median_minutes 2251.99; the bottleneck text gives 2203.6). The note says THROUGHPUT.md is not in the working copy, and a Glob for THROUGHPUT.md found nothing in the snapshot, so the claim is accurate.

criteria.criterion: The note explains how the change removes the bottleneck: the verified job's single landing commit is built on current host main via Git::merge_tree from the job's recorded base, then Git::commit_tree, then pushed, so the local landing branch is no longer a staging area. It says why the stage's wait (the later of the outcome and the newest landing record) shrinks.
criteria.evidence: Section 2 lists the steps: fetch main, merge_tree(base, ours, theirs), commit_tree with main's tip as parent, push, write one landing record. It ends with 'The local landing branch is no longer written to'. Section 3 says one record per job makes 'newest record' equal to 'first record', so the end of the stage stops moving. I checked these against the code: Git::merge_tree(base, ours, theirs) -> Result<Option<String>> (lib.rs:673; None on conflict, as the note says), commit_tree (lib.rs:612), and landing_end = max(outcome, landing_record_time) where landing_record_time takes .max() (throughput.rs:395-413).

criteria.criterion: The note states the predicted saving of 5.0 minutes per landed job and says how the next throughput review measures it: it compares the landing-and-rebuild minutes measured after the change landed with this prediction.
criteria.evidence: Section 5 gives 'Predicted saving: 5.0 minutes per landed job (estimate...)'. The next review takes the landing-and-rebuild median of jobs landed after the change, compares it with 2203.6 and compares the saving with 5.0, leaving out jobs landed before the change. It never says how 'the saving' itself is computed (see the minor finding).

criteria.criterion: The note has alternatives considered, risks and rollback sections. It has an Existing code section that reuses or extends docs/design/per-job-main-landing.md, docs/design/per-job-landing-branches.md, crates/athena-git/src/lib.rs and crates/athena-core/src/land.rs by path, and states what differs from them.
criteria.evidence: Sections 7 (Alternatives considered), 8 (Risks) and 9 (Rollback) are present. Section 4 names all four paths, plus continuous-landing.md, and says what differs for each. The functions it names exist: plan (land.rs:132), resync_tip (218), pr_commits (267), resync_onto_merge (311). The three docs exist.

criteria.criterion: The note says that a change implementing the design must cite throughput review 20261110-024838-mch9 in its request text.
criteria.evidence: Section 6: 'A change that implements this design must cite throughput review `20261110-024838-mch9` in its request text.'

findings.summary: The two notes now give different citation duties for the same design. The new note does not say its citation replaces the one in per-job-main-landing.md §7.
findings.evidence: per-job-main-landing.md §7 still says an implementing change 'must cite throughput review `20261109-014617-5cg0`'. When per-job-main-landing.md replaced the earlier note's citation, it said so and left a pointer in per-job-landing-branches.md §10. The new note's section 4 only says it 'does not rewrite' the older note. Someone implementing the design could cite the old review, and then the next review would not score the mch9 prediction. A sentence in the new note stating that it replaces §7's citation would fix this. That stays inside the deliverables.

findings.summary: The Risks section names land.rs functions that do not do what it claims.
findings.evidence: The note says 'refuse_detached and dispatched_from in land.rs already refuse' a wrong or missing recorded base. In land.rs:86-128, refuse_detached rejects a detached HEAD, and dispatched_from looks up the dispatch branch name. Neither checks the base commit. The base check is `git.is_ancestor(p, head)` in plan (land.rs:159), which returns Plan::Stale.

findings.summary: The push-race risk puts the conflict in the wrong place.
findings.evidence: Section 2 pushes each commit to that job's own pull request branch. A second job's push to a different branch cannot be refused because of the first job's push. The real conflict is when the change is merged into main after main has moved, which per-job-main-landing.md §6 ('Main moved') describes correctly.

findings.summary: The scoring method does not say how 'the saving' is computed, and part of it is undefined.
findings.evidence: Section 5 compares the post-change headline with 2203.6 and 'the saving with the 5.0 minute prediction'. Section 3's 'honest limit' says the headline will fall by much more than the saving, so taking the drop in the headline as the saving would score about 2000 minutes against 5.0. The note mentions 'first-landing time' without defining it and does not adopt per-job-main-landing.md §5's scoring rule (saving = the fall in the first-landing stage). Readers have to infer the rule from the older note.

summary: The change adds docs/design/direct-main-landing.md and one CHANGELOG entry, which are exactly the two expected files. The note cites throughput review 20261110-024838-mch9. Its figures (2203.6 of 2252.0 median minutes, the 1069.2/1537.1/1842.1 trend, the 5.0-minute prediction) match the review record in the evidence snapshot. It also says these were copied from the review because THROUGHPUT.md is absent, which is true in this snapshot. It describes the merge_tree → commit_tree → push design and explains why the stage end stops moving once a job appears in only one landing record. It defines how the next review scores the prediction and has sections for existing code, alternatives, risks, rollback and the citation duty. All five criteria are met. There are four minor findings. (1) The older per-job-main-landing.md §7 still tells an implementing change to cite review 20261109-014617-5cg0, and the new note does not say its own citation replaces that one, so the same design now names two reviews to cite. (2) Under Risks, the note says refuse_detached and dispatched_from guard a wrong or missing recorded base. They don't: they check HEAD and the dispatch branch. The base check is the is_ancestor test in plan. (3) The race risk says a push to a per-job branch is refused when another job pushes first. That conflict actually happens when the change is merged into main, not when it is pushed. (4) Section 5 never defines how "the saving" is computed, and its "honest limit" warns that the headline falls by more than the saving. The older note's scoring rule, which uses the time to the first landing record, is not adopted explicitly. None of these is wrong enough to block a design note.
